title: forensics-evidence-capture-and-siem-export-playbook
content:
Purpose:
This playbook documents the on-call steps and technical commands for: capturing forensic evidence, exporting relevant audit logs to our SIEM, preserving chain-of-custody, and preparing artifacts for a post-incident security postmortem. It is focused on cloud-hosted incidents (GCP/AWS) and self-hosted runtime nodes that Redwood operates for Dedicated/Private customers.

Scope and when to use:
- Use this runbook whenever an incident requires evidence preservation beyond routine logging (suspected breach, data exfiltration, privilege misuse, or unexplained persistent access).
- Not intended for simple application errors or routine debugging. If unsure, escalate to SecOps lead.

Key contacts (on-call rota):
- Primary on-call secops: @secops-oncall (PagerDuty: PD-SEC-ONCALL)
- Forensics SME: Riley Chen (pagerduty: PD-RILEY)
- Cloud infra SRE: Jordan Blake
- Legal/Privacy triage: Morgan Alvarez
- Slack urgent channel: #secops-incident-response

Initial triage checklist (first 30 minutes):
1) Triage and scope: capture initial incident ticket (JIRA key or internal tracking). Assign severity and indicate whether evidence collection is required.
2) Contain if required: apply temporary deny ingress/egress rules, rotate affected service credentials, scale down suspected compromised runners. Note: prefer containment actions that preserve disk/memory state when doing forensics.
3) Notify stakeholders: use incident template (linked artifacts) to notify legal, product security, and customer-success if customer data may be affected.
4) Start evidence log: create an evidence log file (e.g., s3://redwood-sec-evidence/INC-XXXX/chain-of-custody.txt) and record who performed each step, timestamps (UTC), commands run, and hashes of artifacts.

Evidence collection priorities (order matters):
- Volatile memory snapshot (if pod/VM/container suspected): memory is the most ephemeral. If live capture is feasible without destroying evidence, capture memory first.
- Running process and network state (ps, ss/netstat, lsof, conntrack).
- Disk image or selective file copy (files under /var/log, application logs, config files, container overlays).
- Audit and cloud logs (IAM, API gateway, load balancer, cloud trail/Activity Logs).
- SIEM-export: save query results, saved searches, and raw events covering the incident window.

Commands and examples (Linux VM and container hosts):
- Capture memory (host): // Use 'avml' where available or liME for deep capture
  sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y build-essential git && 
  git clone https://github.com/google/avml.git && 
  sudo python3 avml/avml.py /tmp/memory.raw
- Lightweight process snapshot:
  sudo ps auxww > /tmp/ps-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).txt
  sudo ss -tunap > /tmp/ss-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).txt
  sudo lsof -nP > /tmp/lsof-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).txt
- Docker/container evidence (on host):
  sudo docker ps --no-trunc > /tmp/docker-ps.txt
  sudo docker inspect <container-id> > /tmp/container-<id>-inspect.json
  sudo docker logs <container-id> > /tmp/container-<id>-logs.txt
- Kubernetes pod capture (if kubectl context available):
  kubectl get pods -A --output wide > /tmp/k8s-pods-$(date -u +%s).txt
  kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> > /tmp/describe-pod.txt
  kubectl logs --timestamps -n <ns> <pod> --all-containers > /tmp/pod-logs.txt
  kubectl exec -n <ns> <pod> -- ps auxww > /tmp/pod-ps.txt
- Hash artifacts (SHA256):
  sha256sum /tmp/pod-logs.txt > /tmp/pod-logs.txt.sha256

Cloud provider evidence guidance:
- GCP: Export Audit Logs for the time range (Cloud Audit Logs, VPC flow logs). Use the Logs Explorer to run a query and export as newline-delimited JSON. Retain original export in a secure bucket: gs://redwood-sec-evidence/INC-XXXX/gcp-raw-logs/
- AWS: Use CloudTrail lookup events, VPC Flow Logs, and S3 access logs. Use Athena or CLI to run a query and store JSON results in s3://redwood-sec-evidence/INC-XXXX/aws-raw-logs/
- For both: preserve the storage object checksum and IAM policy snapshot.

Audit log schema (canonical fields to capture when exporting from application/service):
- timestamp (ISO8601 UTC)
- service (e.g., api-gateway, auth-service, model-serving)
- environment (hosted|dedicated|private, or region)
- host_id / instance_id / pod_id
- user_id (if authenticated) or api_key_id
- request_id / trace_id
- method / endpoint / route
- response_status
- bytes_in / bytes_out (when available)
- src_ip / dst_ip
- action (e.g., token_create, model_infer, deploy)
- rbac_grant (before/after) when RBAC change events detected
- raw_message (original log line)

SIEM export procedures (current integrations: Splunk, Elastic/Kibana, Chronicle):
- Splunk (on-prem or SaaS):
  1) Use time range in UTC around suspected activity plus buffer (+/- 30m for short events, +/- 48h for persistent activity).
  2) Run saved search or ad-hoc SPL: index=redwood-* (service=* OR host=*) | where request_id=="<id>" OR user_id=="<user>"
  3) Export results as raw events (gzip compressed) and store to secure evidence bucket. Record SPL used.
- Elastic/Kibana:
  1) Create a Discover query matching timeframe and fields above. Add columns timestamp, host, user_id, request_id, action.
  2) Export as NDJSON and save. If sample size is large, export in time-chunked batches (e.g., hourly).
- Google Chronicle: export results using the UI export tool or API; ensure you attach event metadata and query text.

SIEM-specific tips:
- Always export raw events (not just aggregates). Raw events preserve parse errors and nested fields.
- If queries hit cardinality limits, break by host or request_id and re-join offline.
- Preserve the exact query used and timestamps (UTC tz) in the evidence log.

Chain-of-custody and evidence storage:
- Naming convention: INC-<JIRA>-<artifact-type>-<UTC_TS>.ext (e.g., INC-SEC-412-k8s-logs-20250604T153000Z.ndjson.gz)
- Storage: secure bucket with restricted IAM (read: secops+forensics; write: oncall; admin: legal-release). Buckets must enforce encryption at rest and object versioning. Example buckets: s3://redwood-sec-evidence/ or gs://redwood-sec-evidence/
- Metadata: for each object record: original path, collector name, collector host, SHA256, collection command, and collection UTC time. Add this to chain-of-custody file.
- Access: use short-lived signed URLs for sharing with legal/third-party forensic vendors. Record every access in the evidence log.

RBAC and access control guidance during incident:
- Principle: least privilege. Temporarily elevate only the minimal role needed, with documented justification. Use ephemeral roles when possible (STS tokens, short-lived key rotation).
- RBAC changes: any modification to IAM/RBAC that might be related to the incident must be captured (before/after snapshots of policy bindings). Use the RBAC v2 audit exports (link to RBAC v2 schema in Confluence).
- Sensitive exports (logs containing PII): mask or redact only when required by legal; prefer to retain raw copies in a separate secure bucket accessible only to legal+forensics.

Evidence automation hooks (recommended short-lived automations):
- Pre-built Lambda/Cloud Function that, given INC id and time window, will: run saved SIEM queries, bundle results, compute checksums, and move artifacts to secure bucket with metadata JSON.
- Webhook pattern: trigger automation from the incident ticket (JIRA transition) or a Slack slash command (/collect-evidence INC-412 --since 2025-06-01T00:00Z --until 2025-06-04T00:00Z).
- Safeguards: automation must require two-person approval for exports > 100GB or that include customer PII.

When to engage external forensics:
- Confirmed data exfiltration, ransomware, or persistence beyond our containment capabilities.
- When legal advises third-party chain-of-custody certification.

Post-incident evidence checklist (before closing incident):
- All artifacts hashed and checksums stored in chain-of-custody.
- SIEM exports included with query text and timeframe documented.
- RBAC and IAM policy snapshots for the incident timeframe preserved.
- All temporary access (ephemeral roles, rotated keys) revoked and rotation recorded.
- Evidence bucket ACLs reviewed and restricted to minimal principals.
- Forensics/SME sign-off recorded in the incident ticket.

Postmortem template (append to ticket or Confluence):
- Title: concise summary (e.g., "INC-SEC-412: token leak via CI runner")
- Incident owner: (name)
- Severity and impact window: (UTC start/end)
- Summary: 3–4 sentence summary of what happened and impact
- Root cause: technical cause and process/culture contributing factors
- Timeline: ordered timestamps (UTC) of key events and actions taken
- Evidence produced: list of artifacts, locations (bucket path), and checksums
- Remediation actions: code fixes, infra changes, policy changes, owners, and ETA
- Lessons learned / follow-ups: changes to runbooks, automation, RBAC rules, and monitoring
- Postmortem status: draft | reviewed | final

References and related docs:
- Confluence: IR Playbooks (linked_artifacts)
- RBAC v2 schema and audit export guide (search Confluence: "RBAC v2 audit schema")
- SIEM export best practices (internal KB)

Quick decision guide (TL;DR):
- Suspected active compromise: collect volatile memory -> process/network -> full logs -> export SIEM raw events -> preserve chain-of-custody.
- Suspected credential misuse without persistence: capture API gateway logs, auth audit logs, and RBAC change snapshots.
- Large volume/long-running data exfiltration suspicion: escalate to Forensics SME + Legal immediately and limit data movement until a plan is approved.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Finalize Lambda-based evidence export with two-approver flow (owner: Jordan Blake)
- Add automated SIEM saved-search naming convention and registration for evidence exports
- Wire up incident ticket -> automated evidence collection trigger (secure approval flow)

Revision history:
- 2024-11-02: initial draft (Asha Patel)
- 2025-01-15: added SIEM export examples and RBAC guidance (Riley Chen)
- 2025-06-04: updated storage naming conventions and chain-of-custody template (Morgan Alvarez)

End of playbook.
